This discrepancy arises because direct observation lacks statistical robustness. The midparental relationship is asymmetric: while sons deviate 1/3 as much from their midparent as the midparent does from the population mean, the reverse is not true. This asymmetry stems from the fact that the midparent is typically closer to the population mean than either individual parent. The principle of regression toward the mean implies that extreme traits in parents tend to produce offspring closer to the average. Thus, exceptional individuals are more often sons of moderate parents than sons of exceptional parents—a phenomenon rooted in the central limit theorem and variance decomposition. The failure mode lies in assuming symmetry in regression coefficients across directional relationships.
